abstract: Protein kinase MoCK2 has been identified as a pivotal regulator in the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae , orchestrating critical biological processes including hyphal growth, conidiation, and host infection. Building upon our previous investigations into its interplay with cellular energy metabolism and polar regeneration during appressorium formation, this study systematically delineated the MoCK2 regulatory network through integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic analyses. Three key mechanistic insights emerged from this research. Firstly, while MoCK2 deficiency did not directly impair mitochondrial functionality, it disrupted intracellular vesicular trafficking systems, thereby constraining substrate availability for mitochondrial metabolism and ultimately leading to energy homeostasis defects. Secondly, absence of MoCK2 nucleolar localization in regulatory subunit deletion mutants substantially compromised ribosome biogenesis, creating a bottleneck in protein synthesis capacity that failed to meet cellular demands. Thirdly, phosphoregulation analysis demonstrated MoCK2’s multifaceted role as a signaling node, modulating critical developmental transitions through phosphorylation-dependent control of conidial germination, appressorial morphogenesis, and host penetration apparatus assembly. These findings established MoCK2 as a central coordinator linking organelle dynamics, translational regulation, and infection-related signaling cascades. This study provides a conceptual framework for future investigations into the functional characterization of MoCK2, while also offering methodological references for CK2 research across diverse biological systems. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12864-025-12207-3.

Materials and methods
Fungal strains and growth conditions
The
M. oryzae
Ku80 used in this study was provided by Professor Zonghua Wang, Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University. Two isogenic mutants were generated through targeted gene deletion in the Ku80 background strains. The B1 mutant was created by disrupting MGG_00446 (encoding regulatory subunit 1 of MoCK2), while the B2 mutant was developed through deletion of MGG_05651 (encoding regulatory subunit 2 of MoCK2). All experimental strains, including the parental Ku80 and derived mutants B1/B2, were preserved as desiccated cultures on sterile filter paper for long-term storage. For proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis, fungal strains were cultured in liquid complete medium (CM: 0.6% casein hydrolysate, 0.6% yeast extract, 1% sucrose) under standardized conditions (25℃, 130 rpm orbital shaking). Mycelia were harvested after a few days cultivation by filtration, followed by immediate flash-freezing in liquid nitrogen to preserve post-translational modification states prior to omics processing.
Protein extraction
The sample was initially ground using liquid nitrogen, and subsequently, the resultant powder was transferred into a 5-mL centrifuge tube. It was then subjected to sonication for three minutes on ice with a high-intensity ultrasonic processor (Scientz) in a lysis buffer composed of 1% TritonX-100, 10 mM dithiothreitol, 1% protease inhibitor cocktail, 50 µM PR-619, 3 µM TSA, 50 mM NAM, 2 mM EDTA, and 1% phosphatase inhibitor for phosphorylation. Following this, an equal volume of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 8.0) was added to the mixture, which was then vortexed for an additional 5 min. After centrifugation at 4 °C for 10 min at 5,500 g, the upper phenol phase was carefully transferred to a fresh centrifuge tube.
Proteins were precipitated by adding at least four volumes of ammonium sulfate-saturated methanol, and the mixture was incubated at −20 °C for a minimum of 6 h. Following centrifugation at 4 °C for 10 min, the supernatant was discarded. The remaining precipitate was washed three times with ice-cold methanol, followed by ice-cold acetone. The protein was then redissolved in 8 M urea, and its concentration was determined using a BCA kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Trypsin digestion
The sample was gradually introduced to achieve a final concentration of 20% (m/v) TCA, promoting protein precipitation. It was then vortexed to ensure thorough mixing and incubated for 2 h at 4 °C. The precipitate was subsequently collected by centrifuging at 4500 g for 5 min at 4 °C. The precipitated protein underwent three washes with pre-cooled acetone and was dried for 1 min.
Next, the protein sample was redissolved in 200 mM TEAB and ultrasonically dispersed to ensure homogeneity. Trypsin was added at a 1:50 trypsin-to-protein mass ratio for the initial overnight digestion. To further process the sample, it was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol for 30 min at 56 °C and then alkylated with 11 mM iodoacetamide for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Lastly, the peptides were desalted using a Strata X SPE column.
LC–MS/MS analysis
The tryptic peptides were dissolved in solvent A and directly loaded onto a custom-made reversed-phase analytical column with dimensions of 25-cm length and 100 μm inner diameter. The mobile phase comprised solvent A (0.1% formic acid, 2% acetonitrile in water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid, 90% acetonitrile in water). Peptide separation was achieved using the following gradient: 6%−23% B from 0 to 68 min, 23%−32% B from 68 to 82 min, 32%−80% B from 82 to 86 min, and 80% B from 86 to 90 min, all at a consistent flow rate of 500 nl/min on a vanquish neo UPLC system (ThermoFisher Scientific).
The separated peptides were subsequently analyzed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 equipped with a nano-electrospray ion source. An electrospray voltage of 2300 V was applied, and the FAIMS compensate voltage (CV) was set to −45 V and − 65 V. Both precursors and fragments were analyzed at the Orbitrap detector. The full MS scan resolution was configured to 60,000 for a scan range of 400–1200 m/z. The MS/MS scan was set with a fixed first mass of 110 m/z at a resolution of 15,000, and TurboTMT was disabled.
Up to 25 of the most abundant precursors were selected for further MS/MS analyses, with a 20 s dynamic exclusion. High-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) fragmentation was performed at a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 27%. The automatic gain control (AGC) target was set to 100%, with an intensity threshold of 50,000 ions/s and an automatic maximum injection time.
Identification and quantitation of proteins
The resulting MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer search engine (v.2.4). Tandem mass spectra were searched against Blast_
Magnaporthe
_
oryzae
_strains_70 − 15_242507_PR_.
20,230,529.fasta (12794 entries) concatenated with reverse decoy and contaminants database. Trypsin (Full) was specified as cleavage enzyme allowing up to 2 missing cleavages. Min. peptide length was set as 6 and max. number of modification per peptide was set as 3. Mass error was set to 10 ppm for precursor ions and 0.02 Da for fragment ions. Carbamidomethyl on Cys was specified as fixed modification. Oxidation on Met, acetylation on protein N-terminal, met-loss on Met and met-loss + acetyl on Met were specified as variable modification. False discovery rate (FDR) of protein, peptide and PSM was adjusted to < 1%.
body:
Introduction
Rice, serving as the primary staple crop for over half of the global population, plays a critical role in global food security and human sustenance [
1
]. This agricultural significance underscores the necessity of maintaining rice production safety through advanced cultivation management strategies. However, yield and grain quality are continually threatened by biotic stresses, with rice blast disease caused by the ascomycete fungus
Magnaporthe oryzae
representing the most destructive phytopathological challenge [
2
]. The pathogen field propagation predominantly occurs through an asexual cycle characterized by airborne conidial dissemination. Following dispersal via wind and rain vectors, conidia undergo morphogenetic differentiation upon rice leaf surfaces, forming specialized infection structures called appressoria. These dome-shaped cells generate enormous turgor pressure through glycerol accumulation, driving the development of penetration pegs that mechanically breach the host cuticular layer. Subsequent invasive hyphal growth facilitates rapid colonization of plant tissues, with visible elliptical lesions bearing gray centers and dark margins appearing within 4–7 days post-infection. These necrotic lesions subsequently produce secondary conidiophores, completing the disease cycle through spore reinfection [
3
]. Elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying this pathogenic development cycle remains crucial for establishing targeted control measures and durable resistance breeding programs.
Appressorium morphogenesis in
M. oryzae
is coordinately governed by multiple signaling cascades, with particular emphasis on the conserved cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (cAMP-PKA) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathways [
4
,
5
]. The developmental process initiates through surface recognition mechanisms, where conidial-expressed G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) such as PTH11 detect physicochemical cues from rice leaf surfaces [
6
]. Subsequent signal transduction involves the activation of heterotrimeric G proteins that trigger downstream effectors, including adenylate cyclase-mediated conversion of ATP to cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) [
4
,
7
]. This secondary messenger activates PKA through cAMP-binding regulatory subunit dissociation, thereby orchestrating diverse cellular processes essential for infection structure development [
4
]. Parallel to cAMP signaling, the pathogen employs a three-tiered MAPK cascade (Mst11-Mst7-Pmk1) that converges with cAMP-PKA signaling to regulate appressorium differentiation through phosphorylation-mediated control of morphogenetic regulators [
8
]. Genetic disruption of either signaling axis could hinder the appressorial formation and pathogenic capacity, underscoring their non-redundant roles in host invasion.
The ontogenic progression from appressorium initiation to functional maturation in
M. oryzae
involves multidimensional reorganization encompassing cellular reprogramming, enzymatic activation, and cytoskeletal remodeling. Following initial stages, autophagy mediates cytoplasmic remodeling in conidia and germ tubes, systematically mobilizing bioenergetic resources into the developing appressorium [
9
]. Simultaneously, melanin undergoes controlled deposition within the appressorial cell wall, driven by osmolyte (glycerol)-mediated turgor dynamics [
10
]. The osmosensing histidine kinase MoSln1 subsequently detects these hydrostatic changes, initiating a negative feedback loop that downregulates both melanogenesis and glycerol biosynthesis to establish polarized maturation states [
11
]. Mechanistically, MoSln1 orchestrates the PKC1-mediated cell wall integrity pathway to activate the Nox2/NoxR NADPH oxidase complex, which facilitates the hierarchical assembly of Septin GTPases into a cortical ring structure at the appressorial pore [
12
,
13
]. These morphogenetic scaffolds dynamically colocalize with F-actin networks through coordinated interactions with ERM (ezrin-radixin-moesin) family proteins that bridge membrane-actin interfaces, while BAR domain-containing effectors concurrently modulate membrane curvature via lipid bilayer deformation [
14
]. The Septin macroassembly functions as a regulatory scaffold that orchestrates two critical cellular processes, including spatially recruiting Exocyst complexes to coordinate site-specific vesicle trafficking, and locally activating cell wall biosynthesis machinery through stabilization of chitin and glucan synthase complexes [
11
,
15
]. This integrated mechanochemical signaling cascade ultimately coordinates actin-driven protrusive force generation with cell wall remodeling to establish the penetration peg, thereby completing host cuticle breaching and infection establishment.
The casein kinase MoCK2 represents a phylogenetically conserved Ser/Thr kinase complex characterized by a heterotetrameric architecture comprising two catalytic subunits paired with two regulatory partners [
16
]. Functionally, this pleiotropic regulatory kinase exhibits constitutive activity within cellular environments, orchestrating a multifaceted regulatory network through phosphorylation of diverse substrate proteins [
17
,
18
]. Its mechanistic repertoire spans multiple regulatory tiers, orchestrating cell cycle progression through cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) signaling dynamics; maintaining cellular homeostasis by balancing proliferation-differentiation transitions; coordinating nucleic acid metabolism through chromatin remodeling and RNA biogenesis pathways; entraining circadian clock synchronization mechanisms; and enforcing proteostasis via integrated regulation of apoptosis signaling and ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) coordination [
19
]. Notably, MoCK2 functions as a molecular nexus integrating temporal and spatial signaling inputs to maintain cellular integrity across kingdoms.
Previous studies have established that MoCK2 plays a critical role in
M. oryzae
, regulating mycelial growth, conidiation, and pathogenicity [
20
]. Transcriptomic profiling further demonstrated that MoCK2 modulated energy metabolism in this fungal pathogen. Mutants lacking the two regulatory subunits of MoCK2 (B1 and B2) exhibited varying reductions in energy conversion processes, particularly in glucose and fatty acid metabolism, demonstrating a significant association between MoCK2 and mitochondrial function. Moreover, both B1 and B2 mutants showed marked decreases in expression levels of multiple mitochondrial function-related genes [
21
]. This observation was corroborated by GFP-MoCKa pull-down assays (MoCKa being the catalytic subunit of MoCK2), which identified numerous mitochondria-associated proteins interacting with the complex [
22
]. These collective findings strongly suggested that MoCK2 was essential for maintaining normal mitochondrial function within the fungal cytoplasm.
Subcellular localization analysis demonstrated that GFP-MoCK2 fusion proteins exhibited pan-cellular distribution in both mycelia and conidia. Fluorescence quantification revealed two primary sites of strongest signal accumulation: nuclear compartments and septal pore regions. Nuclear analysis showed distinct subnuclear partitioning, with nucleolar fluorescence intensity exceeding that observed in the nucleoplasm. At hyphal septa, the fusion proteins displayed bilateral localization flanking the septal pores, forming distinct plug-like structures [
20
]. This dual localization pattern implies potential regulatory roles for MoCK2 in nuclear processes and intercellular communication mechanisms.
Comparative localization analysis revealed that MoCK2 in appressoria exhibited conserved localization patterns with those observed in mycelia and conidia, while demonstrating striking developmental-stage-specific features. During early appressorium development (0–12 h post-induction), GFP-MoCK2 fluorescence was predominantly localized to nuclei. Remarkably, upon reaching maturation, the fusion protein underwent structural reorganization within the appressorial cytoplasm, forming a characteristic annular architecture termed CK2-HRS (MoCK2 Holoenzyme Ring Structure). This unique structure showed spatially coordinated positioning relative to the Septin ring at the appressorial base, maintaining orthogonal positioning throughout its formation [
20
,
23
].
A key temporal distinction emerged between the Septin ring formation and CK2-HRS development. Previous studies established that Septin proteins undergo progressive assembly into a basal ring structure at 4 h post-appressorium induction, precisely positioned at the host-contact interface [
14
]. This Septin scaffold subsequently serves as a platform for recruiting Exocyst components and other factors to orchestrate penetration plug assembly [
15
]. In contrast, CK2-HRS manifested later during appressorium maturation, emerging as a cytoplasmic ring structure after 12 hpi [
23
]. While the spatiotemporal coordination between these structures is evident, the molecular mechanisms governing MoCK2 aggregation into CK2-HRS, including potential regulatory kinases, spatial cues, or post-translational modifications mediating holoenzyme assembly, remain to be elucidated.
Genetic dissection revealed the structural dependency of CK2-HRS formation. When the regulatory subunit of MoCK2 was deleted, CK2-HRS assembly was completely abolished, with GFP-MoCKa fluorescence retaining nuclear localization [
20
]. Consistent with this phenomenon, Septin-mutant (
ΔMosep3
) and Exocyst-mutant (
ΔMoexo70
) strains similarly exhibited CK2-HRS dissolution [
23
]. The disruption of CK2-HRS affected pathogenicity, with B1, B2,
ΔMosep3
mutants losing pathogenicity, and
ΔMoexo70
also significantly reducing pathogenicity, indicating a close correlation between presence of CK2-HRS and pathogenicity formation in
M. oryzae
[
14
,
23
,
24
]. However, the mechanistic basis underlying CK2-HRS mediated infection, particularly its potential roles in signal transduction, effector secretion, or mechanical force generation, remains undefined, leaving the precise molecular orchestration of this holoenzyme ring in pathogenesis unresolved.
Building upon the established role of MoCK2 in pathogenicity, this study implemented a systematic interrogation of its pleiotropic functions through integrated multi-omics profiling. By synergizing phosphoproteomic signatures with functional genetics, we delineated previously unrecognized regulatory dimensions of MoCK2 spanning mitochondrial homeostasis, ribosome biogenesis fidelity, and signal transduction cascades. This multilayered evidence not only significantly broadens the known functional spectrum of MoCK2 but also systematically elucidates previously pathogenic mechanisms by delineating novel molecular connections between MoCK2 activity and developmental pathogenesis in
M. oryzae
.
Results
Proteomics data in B1 and B2 mutants
To systematically investigate the regulatory role of protein kinase MoCK2 in pathogenic development of
M. oryzae
, we performed comparative proteomic profiling of wild-type Ku80 and MoCK2 regulatory subunit deletion mutants (B1/B2). A triplicate biological replication design was implemented across all experimental groups (Ku80 parental strain and B1/B2 mutants), generating nine distinct samples designated as Ku80_ [
1
–
3
], B1_ [
1
–
3
], and B2_ [
1
–
3
] for subsequent proteomic characterization. Rigorous quality control through SDS-PAGE confirmed high-quality protein preparations across all samples, demonstrating high-integrity protein profiles suitable for downstream analyses (Fig.S1). The validated protein extracts underwent parallel processing for global proteome and phosphoproteome investigation. These proteins were subjected to enzyme digestion and LC-MS/MS analysis, and the Proteome Discoverer search engine (v.2.4) was used to retrieve the MS data of each sample for protein identification and quantitative analysis (Table S1) [
25
].
Pearson correlation coefficient analysis of protein expression abundance levels across samples revealed a striking consistency among the three samples in each group, solidifying the reliability of the sequencing data (Fig.S2A) [
26
]. Additionally, we also conducted a principal component analysis (PCA) on the protein abundance values of nine samples [
27
]. The results indicated that there were significant differences in protein abundance between the B1, B2 mutants and the background strains Ku80. PC1 accounted for 41.0% of the variance, suggesting that the disparities in protein expression abundance among different group strains stemmed from the deletion of MoCK2 regulatory subunits. Furthermore, PC2, which explained 20.8% of the variance, indicated that there were sequencing differences even among samples from the same group (Fig.S2B). Our meticulous analysis identified a total of 463,257 matched spectra, 53,986 unique peptides, and 4843 quantifiable proteins in the proteomics data (Fig.S3).
In our proteomic analysis, proteins demonstrating statistically significant differential expression between mutants and parental strains were identified using dual thresholds of
P
< 0.05 and absolute fold change >1.5. Comparative analysis revealed distinct expression profiles between B1 mutants (481 up-regulated and 682 down-regulated proteins) and B2 mutants (262 up-regulated and 289 down-regulated proteins) relative to the Ku80 background strains, as visualized through volcano plots (Fig.
1
and Table S1). Hierarchical clustering analysis further confirmed the consistency of these differential expression patterns across triplicate biological samples (Fig.S4) [
28
]. The observed proteomic perturbations were likely attributable to functional impairment of the MoCK2 holoenzyme due to regulatory subunit deletion. This enzymatic dysfunction appeared to induce systemic protein abundance alterations that drive cellular metabolic reprogramming, potentially explaining the pronounced phenotypic abnormalities characteristic of both B1 and B2 mutants.

) compared with background strains Ku80. The blue points represented downregulated proteins in both mutants compared with Ku80. The red points represented upregulated proteins in both mutants compared with Ku80. Proteins with

values < 0.05 and absolute fold change values > 1.5 were considered to be significantly differentially expressed proteins (DEPs)
KEGG and GO enrichment of down deps in B1 or B2 mutants
To elucidate the precise regulatory mechanism of MoCK2, we performed functional characterization of the differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) through systematic bioinformatic analysis. Initial investigation involved KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) pathway enrichment analysis of DEPs conducted using TBtools, with particular focus on proteins exhibiting reduced expression (down-regulated DEPs) in both B1 and B2 mutants [
29
]. These down-regulated proteins were prioritized for analysis as potential downstream effectors in the MoCK2-mediated regulatory network. Comprehensive functional annotation of these targets was implemented to establish their biological relevance, providing critical insights into the mechanistic basis of MoCK2 regulatory function. This strategic approach enabled systematic identification of key pathways potentially governed by the MoCK2 holoenzyme, advancing our understanding of its role in cellular regulation.
KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed distinct metabolic perturbations associated with the DEPs in each mutant. In B2 mutants, the down-DEPs showed predominant enrichment in fundamental biological processes, specifically energy metabolism and cellular signaling transduction pathways. Notably affected pathways included lipid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and the MAPK signaling pathway (Fig.
2
A and Table S2). Parallel analysis of B1 mutants demonstrated broader functional impacts, with down-DEPs significantly enriched in four major metabolic domains, including carbohydrate metabolism (6 enriched pathways), protein/amino acid metabolism (10 enriched pathways), lipid metabolism (4 enriched pathways), and diverse secondary metabolic processes (14 enriched pathways) (Fig.
2
B and Table S3). This comparative analysis highlighted both shared and distinct regulatory effects mediated through MoCK2 holoenzyme activity in both mutants.

The enriched KEGG terms in green color represented pathways relating to carbohydrate metabolism; the red color showed the pathways associated with lipid metabolism; the pathways involved in amino acid metabolism showed in light blue; the yellow color indicated some secondary metabolism-related pathways
To further elucidate the functional spectrum of protein kinase MoCK2, we performed Gene Ontology (GO) analysis on down-regulated DEPs. The results demonstrated substantial convergence with KEGG enrichment findings in B2 mutants, particularly within energy metabolism pathways. Key enriched biological processes included cellular lipid metabolic process (GO:0044255) and carbohydrate metabolic process (GO:0005975) (Fig.
3
A and Table S2). To our surprise, a subset of down-regulated DEPs in B2 mutants was functionally associated with cellular morphogenesis and developmental regulation, specifically impacting cellular polarity regeneration and cell wall biogenesis (Fig.
3
B and Table S2). These processes were critical for fungal morphogenesis and host invasion. These observations were consistent with our previous research results, namely that the disruption of the CK2-HRS ring structure would impair the regeneration of appressorial polarity and the formation of penetration peg, thereby verifying the functional correlation of these proteomic changes.

In analysis of B1 mutants, down-regulated proteins similarly exhibited enrichment in core metabolic pathways including amino acid metabolism, carbohydrate metabolism, and lipid metabolism (Fig.
3
C-E and Table S3). While sharing these metabolic regulatory signatures with B2 mutants, the B1 proteomic profile revealed expanded functional impacts, suggesting both conserved and isoform-specific regulatory roles within the MoCK2 holoenzyme complex. The coordinated dysregulation of these fundamental metabolic and developmental processes provides a molecular framework for understanding the pleiotropic phenotypic consequences observed in both mutants.
Previous transcriptome studies demonstrated that MoCK2 deficiency significantly affects energy metabolism in
M. oryzae
[
21
]. This conclusion was further corroborated by KEGG and GO analyses of downregulated DEPs in the proteomic data, revealing MoCK2 critical involvement in fundamental metabolic processes including carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism. These findings collectively indicated that MoCK2 dysfunction substantially disrupted cellular energy metabolism in the fungal pathogen. Considering the essential role of mitochondrial function in energy metabolism, we subsequently examined mitochondrial integrity in mutants. Proteomic profiling of B1 mutants showed significant downregulation of proteins associated with two key mitochondrial components, the membrane structural framework and redox-coupled respiratory chain complexes (Fig.
3
F and Table S3). This molecular evidence strongly suggested that MoCK2 deficiency compromised mitochondrial functional integrity, ultimately leading to disrupted energy homeostasis. The resultant metabolic impairment likely contributed to the observed severe phenotypic defects in B1 mutants.
KEGG and GO enrichment of up deps in B1 or B2 mutants
The absence of protein kinase MoCK2 altered the physiological and biochemical state of
M. oryzae
, resulting in the down-regulation of certain proteins and a subsequent decrease in cellular energy metabolism. However, a significant proportion of proteins demonstrated marked upregulation in their expression profiles. To elucidate the role of these up-regulated proteins, we also conducted a thorough analysis, aiming to refine our understanding of the regulatory network pathways associated with MoCK2.
KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed distinct proteomic alterations between B1 and B2 mutants. In the B2 mutant, 17 significantly upregulated proteins were mainly aggregated in the amino acid metabolic pathway (B 09105 Amino acid metabolism), among which 5 proteins were enriched in the tyrosine metabolic pathway (00350 Tyrosine metabolism). Additionally, 6 upregulated proteins demonstrated specific association with nucleotide and purine metabolism (B 09104 Nucleotide metabolism) (Fig.
4
A and Table S2). In contrast, B1 mutants displayed distinct functional clustering, with upregulated proteins showing significant enrichment in transcriptional regulation, RNA processing, and translation-related pathways including ribosome biogenesis (Fig.
4
B and Table S3).
Fig. 4

A

B

C

D

Consistent with KEGG findings, GO enrichment analysis further delineated these functional divergences. For B2 mutants, the upregulated proteome was significantly associated with transcriptional modulation (GO:0045449), RNA processing (GO:0006396), and post-translational protein modification (GO:0043687), alongside metabolic regulation of cellular organic compounds (Fig.
4
C and Table S2). Remarkably, B1 mutants showed highly specific enrichment in GO term enrichment, with virtually all upregulated proteins mapping to RNA transcription (GO:0006351) and translation-related processes (GO:0006412). This pronounced enrichment underscores the key of MoCK2 in orchestrating fundamental genetic information flow, including transcriptional regulation, mRNA maturation, and ribosomal assembly (Fig.
4
D and Table S3).
The elevated protein expression observed in B1 and B2 mutants may be attributed to a compensatory cellular response. Proteomic profiling demonstrated significant enrichment of up-regulated proteins in nucleic acid metabolic pathways, particularly ribosomal biosynthesis processes. This finding aligned with the established nuclear dynamics of MoCK2 holoenzyme in
M. oryzae
, which normally exhibits nucleolar specificity through its regulatory subunits. Crucially, deletion of any regulatory subunit caused complete ablation of nucleolar localization of MoCK2 homoenzyme, suggesting functional impairment of the kinase complex in nuclear subcompartmentalization [
20
]. The nucleolus, a specialized nuclear subdomain comprising rRNA, rDNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, orchestrates three fundamental biological processes, containing maintenance of rRNA gene repositories, transcription/processing of rRNA, and assembly of ribosomal subunits [
30
]. In both B1 and B2 mutants, the impaired nucleolar targeting of MoCK2 kinase complex mechanistically disrupted ribosomal biogenesis pathways. This nucleolar exclusion defect correlated with pronounced upregulation of ribosomal metabolism-associated proteins, indicative of cellular compensation through enhanced translational machinery production to counteract compromised ribosome assembly capacity.
Phosphoproteomics data in B1 and B2 mutants
Previous studies have confirmed that MoCK2 functions as a tetrameric protein kinase complex in
M. oryzae
. Our genetic analysis through targeted deletion of its two distinct regulatory subunits revealed significant alterations in MoCK2 kinase activity [
20
]. This perturbation led to substantial changes in protein phosphorylation patterns when comparing B1 and B2 mutants with background strains Ku80. The observed phosphorylation profile variations, particularly in key signaling pathways, strongly suggested that MoCK2-mediated phosphorylation events played a regulatory role in fungal pathogenicity. Further investigation into the specific phosphorylation targets and signaling networks could elucidate the molecular mechanism underlying MoCK2 regulation of infection-related development in this phytopathogenic fungus.
Proteins from the nine samples were extracted, digested, and analyzed by mass spectrometry. The obtained mass spectrum data were retrieved using Proteome Discoverer (v2.4), and the corresponding proteins phosphorylation sites and peptide segments were shown in Table S4 [
25
].
Inter-group Pearson correlation analysis of phosphoproteomic profiles demonstrated strong intra-group reproducibility across biological replicates (‌Fig.S5A). This high inter-sample homogeneity within experimental groups underscores the robustness of our quantitative phosphoproteomics dataset. Multivariate analysis of phosphoproteomic profiles through principal component analysis (PCA) revealed pronounced segregation patterns among experimental groups, with B1/B2 mutants clustering distinctly from parental Ku80 strains in the PCA plot (‌Fig.S5B‌). The first principal component (PC1, 38.5% variance) primarily captured phosphorylation state differences attributable to regulatory subunit deletions, quantitatively confirming MoCK2’s central role in maintaining phosphoproteome homeostasis. The second principal component (PC2) accounted for 21.9% of the variance, suggesting that there were also sequencing differences present among samples from the same group. These differences could be due to biological variation within the group, such as differences in growth conditions or genetic variation between individual samples.
Our high-resolution mass spectrometry-based phosphoproteomic profiling identified 18,692 unique phosphopeptides containing 17,399 putative phosphorylation sites through MaxQuant processing [
31
]. Following rigorous filtering using Andromeda search engine parameters, 14,028 high-confidence modified peptides were retained with unambiguous site localization probabilities [
32
]. Within this dataset, 12,430 phosphorylation sites met the criteria for reliable quantitative comparison across biological replicates. Subsequent mapping to the
M. oryzae
reference proteome identified 3,877 phosphoproteins, of which 2,774 passed stringent quantification thresholds for subsequent differential phosphorylation analysis (Fig.S6).
Using the previously established DEP selection criteria, we identified a total of 1734 phosphoproteins with differential abundance. Among these, 835 were found to be up-regulated and 899 down-regulated in B1 mutants when compared to the background strains Ku80. Simultaneously, in B2 mutants, 909 phosphorylated proteins exhibited changes in expression abundance, with 237 being up-regulated and 672 down-regulated. Our phosphoproteomic profiling prioritized the identification of dynamic phosphorylation events across experimental conditions. Quantitative analysis revealed significant alterations in phosphorylation patterns between mutant strains, with B1 mutants demonstrating 1,480 hyperphosphorylated sites and 1,724 hypophosphorylated sites. Similarly, B2 mutants exhibited 342 upregulated phosphorylation events contrasted by 1,104 downregulated sites (Fig.
5
A-C and Table S5). The phosphorylation intensity profiles for both enhanced and attenuated sites showed high reproducibility across triplicate experimental groups (
n
= 9), as evidenced by tight clustering in correlation analyses (Fig.
5
D).

We performed comprehensive motif analysis of phosphorylation site microenvironments using the MEME Suite platform with motif-X algorithm implementation [
33
]. This computational approach enabled systematic identification of evolutionarily conserved phosphorylation motifs. Our findings revealed that serine and threonine phosphorylation accounted for nearly all the localized phosphorylation sites, with serine motifs occurring at a higher frequency. In total, 76 phosphoserine motifs and 25 phosphothreonine motifs were identified during this experiment (Table S5). Interestingly, four proline-directed phosphorylation motifs emerged as the most statistically significant signatures: [RPx_T_P], [Rxx_T_PP], [Rxx_S_PxP], and [RxP_S_P], all containing canonical (-S/T-P-) recognition patterns characteristic of proline-directed kinases (Fig.S7).
Comprehensive analysis of proteomics and phosphoproteomics data in B1 and B2 mutants
To investigate the potential correlation between protein expression changes and phosphorylation dynamics, we performed an integrated analysis of proteomic and phosphoproteomic datasets from B1 and B2 mutants. Our results demonstrated that phosphorylation alterations in both mutants were predominantly independent of corresponding protein abundance changes. Detailed quantification revealed distinct regulatory patterns between the two mutants. In B1 mutants, 56 upregulated and 68 downregulated phosphoproteins exhibited concomitant changes at both the expression and phosphorylation levels, representing only 6% (56/933) and 7% (68/971) of total upregulated and downregulated phosphoproteins, respectively (Fig.
6
A and Table S6). B2 mutants showed even more pronounced dissociation between these regulatory layers, with merely 4% (11/275) of upregulated and 3% (25/833) of downregulated phosphoproteins demonstrating coordinated expression-phosphorylation changes (Fig.
6
B and Table S6). This comprehensive analysis established that post-translational phosphorylation modifications operate largely independently of transcriptional/translational regulation in both mutants.

Furthermore, through in-depth analysis, we identified that proteins with phosphorylation changes in both B1 and B2 mutants contained multiple phosphorylation sites within their sequences. Intriguingly, certain sites on the same protein exhibited increased phosphorylation levels, while others showed decreased phosphorylation, indicating a lack of unified up- or down-regulation trends. These proteins may perform complex physiological functions in cells. However, in this study, we specifically focused on individual proteins whose phosphorylation changes displayed a unified directional trend across all their sites. Specifically, in B1 mutants, 429 proteins demonstrated enhanced phosphorylation levels, whereas 475 proteins exhibited reduced phosphorylation levels. Similarly, in B2 mutants, 138 proteins showed increased phosphorylation, while 547 proteins displayed decreased phosphorylation (Fig.
6
A, B and Table S6).
Through systematic investigation of phosphorylation-altered proteins in MoCK2-deficient strains and their molecular interplay with MoCK2, this study aimed to elucidate the intrinsic regulatory mechanisms by which the MoCK2 kinase governs pathogenicity in
M. oryzae
.
Analysis of phosphoproteins involving in mitochondrial metabolism
In our previous proteomics analysis, we observed significant suppression of energy metabolism in both B1 and B2 mutants of
M. oryzae
, manifested by substantial downregulation of multiple proteins involved in this pathway (Table S2). Besides, a subset of these DEPs exhibited mitochondrial localization and were directly associated with energy production processes, suggesting a functional link between MoCK2 activity and mitochondrial metabolism. However, subsequent phosphoproteomic profiling revealed that most proteins showing altered phosphorylation patterns in the mutants were not primarily localized to mitochondria (Fig.
6
C, D and Table S6). This observation implied that MoCK2 deficiency might not directly impair mitochondrial enzymatic functions through phosphorylation-mediated regulation. The observed results reveal a paradoxical phenomenon: despite apparent impairment in mitochondrial energy metabolism within the mutants, the underlying mechanism appears to operate independently of direct phosphorylation regulation of mitochondrial proteins‌. This dichotomy prompted further investigation into alternative regulatory pathways through which MoCK2 may influence mitochondrial function and cellular energy homeostasis.
Mitochondria, as double-membrane enclosed organelles, maintain strict regulation of molecular transit through specialized transport systems. The proper functioning of these organelles depends not only on intrinsic enzymatic activities but also on efficient delivery of substrates via passive diffusion or active transport mechanisms. Compromised transporters would consequently impair mitochondrial bioenergetics through substrate deprivation.
Phosphoproteomic profiling revealed significant enrichment of membrane trafficking among proteins exhibiting decreased phosphorylation in both mutants. Quantitative analysis identified 52 and 57 membrane trafficking related phosphoproteins with reduced modification levels in B1 and B2 mutants respectively (Fig.
7
A, B and Table S7). Further GO enrichment analysis revealed that the deletion of MoCK2 in the mutant caused significant alterations in protein phosphorylation predominantly enriched in transport processes. Specifically, the B1 mutant exhibited downregulation of phosphorylation in 90 proteins and upregulation in 66 proteins, while the B2 mutant showed phosphorylation downregulation in 122 proteins (Fig.
7
C, D and Table S7).

Interestingly, these findings align with our previous transcriptomic data indicating dysregulation of sugar transporter-encoding genes in both B1 and B2 mutants [

]. Multi-omics integration demonstrates that MoCK2 deficiency disrupts cellular logistics through dual synergistic pathways: transcriptional dysregulation of substrate transporters and post-translational phosphorylation modifications. This dual alteration compromises metabolite transport and mitochondrial membrane shuttling, establishing a substrate-depleted mitochondrial microenvironment that ultimately impairs energy metabolism. Importantly, these findings positioned the observed mitochondrial dysfunction as an indirect consequence of systemic transport defects, rather than primary damage to mitochondrial enzymatic systems.
Analysis of phosphoproteins involving in signal transduction
In the preceding discussion, we have elucidated that the protein kinase MoCK2 played a central regulatory role in cellular processes. Through interaction with multiple substrates, MoCK2 participated in various signal transduction pathways and influenced the progression of physiological and biochemical activities within the cell. Therefore, when analyzing altered protein phosphorylation patterns in mutant strains, our primary focus remained on signal transduction mechanisms. We aimed to decipher the regulatory network of MoCK2 by systematically investigating proteins exhibiting phosphorylation-dependent interactions with MoCK2.
Our initial observation revealed phosphorylation downregulated proteins in both mutant strains. KEGG enrichment analysis demonstrated significant clustering of these proteins within signal transduction pathways. In the B1 mutant strain, phosphorylation-downregulated proteins were significantly enriched in multiple signaling pathways, including
B09132
Signal transduction, 01001 Protein kinases, 04070 Phosphatidylinositol signaling system, and 04011 MAPK signaling pathway. Comparatively, the B2 mutant exhibited reduced phosphorylation levels of proteins involved in both
B09132
Signal transduction and 04011 MAPK signaling pathway (Fig.
7
A, B and Table S7). Furthermore, GO enrichment analysis demonstrated that the deletion of MoCK2 altered the MAPK signaling pathway in B1 and B2 mutant (Fig.
8
A, B and Table S8). Among the proteins enriched in MAPK pathway in B1 and B2 mutants, three protein kinases, MST20 (Serine/threonine-protein kinase MST20,
Q7Z8E9
, MGG_12821), MST11 (mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase MST11, G4N7 × 0, MGG_14847) and MST7 (mitogen-activated protein kinase MST7,
G4NEB8
, MGG_00800), were of particular interest. These kinases were upstream of PMK1 playing a crucial role in regulating the formation of appressorium in
M. oryzae
[
8
]. Therefore, the decrease in their phosphorylation level likely contributed to reduce PMK1 function and pathogenicity. Recent research has shown that MST7 interacted with ARylatio-modified 14-3-3 family proteins [
34
]. We also found that the phosphorylation level of 14-3-3 family protein (G4MTW6, MGG_01588) also decreased in B1 mutants. These results suggested that MoCK2 could affect the phosphorylation of MST20, MST11, MST7, and 14-3-3 to regulate the function of PMK1 and the pathogenicity formation. In addition to affecting the MAPK pathway, we also found that the phosphorylation levels of proteins associated with the cAMP signaling pathway were affected. Specifically, the phosphorylation levels of adenylyl cyclase-associated protein, AGC/PKA protein kinase (G4N7T3, MGG_06368), and cAMP-independent regulatory protein pac2 (G4N6D4, MGG_06564) were down-regulated. The results above indicated that the protein kinase MoCK2 was involved in intracellular signal transduction by influencing the cAMP or MAPK signaling pathways in cells.

In addition, alongside the proteins exhibiting downregulated phosphorylation, our analysis revealed several proteins showing upregulated phosphorylation patterns in the mutant strains. The cell surface sensor SHO1 (
Q2KEW0
, MGG_09125) was identified as a critical molecular switch governing rice leaf epidermal recognition, demonstrating its indispensable role in plant-pathogen interactions [

]. Protein kinase C (G4NFW8, MGG_08689) emerged as a central signaling hub that orchestrates transmembrane signaling through Ca²⁺-mediated signal integration, phosphorylation-dependent activation of downstream effectors, and cross-talk with other signaling pathways [
12
]. These two signaling components function as upstream regulators within the signaling cascade and likely modulate MoCK2 expression through yet-to-be-characterized molecular mechanisms‌.
These findings demonstrate that protein kinase MoCK2 played a crucial role in cell signaling, and its functional disruption impaired signal transduction, leading to dysregulation of physiological and biochemical processes, ultimately resulting in severe phenotypic defects in B1 and B2 mutants.
Discussion
Protein kinase MoCK2 has been identified as a critical regulator in the pathogenesis of
M. oryzae
, the causal agent of rice blast disease. Previous investigations have demonstrated that MoCK2 orchestrates multiple essential biological processes in this phytopathogenic fungus, including vegetative growth, conidiogenesis, and pathogenic development [
20
]. Transcriptomic profiling of MoCK2 regulatory subunit deletion mutants (named with B1 and B2 mutants respectively) revealed substantial impairment in energy metabolism pathways, which likely contributes to the observed severe phenotypic abnormalities such as reduced conidiation and compromised host infection capacity [
21
]. To systematically elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying MoCK2-mediated regulation of fungal pathogenicity, this study employed integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic approaches. These complementary strategies aimed to delineate the kinase functional targets and reconstruct its comprehensive regulatory network, thereby providing mechanistic insights into MoCK2-dependent virulence establishment in this economically significant plant pathogen.
Integrated proteomic profiling demonstrated that B1 and B2 mutants exhibited significant downregulation of energy metabolism-related proteins, corroborating previous transcriptomic evidence of compromised mitochondrial functionality. These findings supported our hypothesis that MoCK2 deficiency disrupted mitochondrial homeostasis through phosphorylation-dependent mechanisms. Building upon our prior proposition that MoCK2-mediated phosphorylation maintains substrate proteins in an unfolded conformation to facilitate membrane translocation, current data reveal impaired transmembrane transport efficiency in both mutants, a phenomenon attributable to deficient phosphorylation signals in the absence of functional MoCK2 [
22
]. Given the architectural constraints imposed by mitochondrial double membrane systems, which necessitate specialized transport mechanisms, we hypothesize that CK2 phosphorylation enables non-folded protein transit across membranes. This model implies the existence of mitochondrial phosphatases responsible for dephosphorylating imported proteins to restore native folding states. Intriguingly, our phosphoproteomic screens identified tyrosine phosphatase G4N373 (MGG_04942), a mitochondrial-localized enzyme displaying reduced phosphorylation in B1 mutants, as a potential collaborator in this regulatory cascade. This observation raises critical questions regarding coordinated kinase-phosphatase interactions governing mitochondrial protein trafficking. Our subsequent investigations will specifically address whether G4N373 partners with MoCK2 to mediate phosphorylation-dependent protein transport dynamics. Systematic characterization of mitochondrial phosphatase networks, particularly their functional interplay with CK2 signaling, promises to unveil novel regulatory nodes connecting post-translational modifications with organellar proteostasis in fungal pathogenesis.
Comparative proteomic profiling revealed a paradoxical upregulation of ribosomal biogenesis-related proteins in both MoCK2 mutants, despite their overall impairment in energy metabolism pathways. This elevation in ribosomal components coincided with the characteristic nucleolar localization deficiency of MoCK2 in mutant strains, a phenotype critically affecting ribosome assembly. The observed protein upregulation likely represents compensatory responses to ribosomal biogenesis defects caused by disrupted nucleoplasmic partitioning of translation machinery components. However, these compensatory mechanisms ultimately failed to restore functional ribosome pools, as evidenced by persistent deficiencies in ribosomal RNA processing and subunit maturation. This molecular imbalance resulted in inadequate protein synthesis capacity that compromised fundamental cellular processes, particularly those requiring rapid protein turnover during host invasion and stress adaptation in
M. oryzae
.
During rice infection by
M. oryzae
, extensive protein aggregation orchestrated critical developmental processes including penetration peg formation and appressorial polarity regeneration. The infection cascade initiated with Sln1 protein-mediated recognition of appressorial turgor pressure, triggering sequential recruitment of the Nox complex and Septin proteins at the appressorial base to establish the penetration site [
11
]. Subsequent assembly of the Exocyst complex around Septin structures facilitated targeted protein secretion essential for host invasion [
15
]. Multiple functional protein clusters converge within mature appressoria, including cell polarity regulators (ERM protein TEA1), phosphoinositide metabolism enzymes (STT4 PtdIns-4-kinase and MSS4 PtdIns-4-phosphate 5-kinase), membrane curvature mediators (I-BAR protein Rvs167), and actin polymerization components (WASP/Arp2/3 complex protein Las17) [
14
]. These coordinated molecular events demonstrated the requirement for elaborate protein networks during appressorial maturation and polarized growth. Crucially, MoCK2 emerged as a central regulator of infection competence through its essential role in ribosomal function. MoCK2-deficient appressoria exhibited severe ribosomal defects that impaired protein biosynthesis, consequently disrupting the infection process. This established MoCK2 as a pivotal molecular checkpoint ensuring proper protein synthesis capacity for successful host colonization by
M. oryzae
.
Following Exocyst complex assembly at the appressorial base, the CK2-HRS structure formed during the advanced stage of infection when protein aggregation reached peak levels and penetration peg initiation became evident [
23
]. This temporal coordination suggested CK2-HRS served as a molecular scaffold sustaining polarized growth mechanisms essential for host invasion. Mechanistically, integrated proteomic and phosphoproteomic profiling revealed significant downregulation of polarity-related proteins and their phosphorylation states in MoCK2 mutants. Specifically, disrupted maintenance of appressorial polarity manifested as defective penetration peg morphogenesis and diminished fungal virulence. These results positioned CK2 as a master regulatory kinase governing polarity homeostasis through phosphorylation-dependent control of effector networks, ultimately determining
M. oryzae
pathogenic success.
The developmental progression of
M. oryzae
, encompassing conidiogenesis, conidial germination, appressorium maturation, and host penetration, operated through tightly coordinated signaling hierarchies. At the initiation stage, conidial production demonstrated strict regulatory control, as evidenced by phenotypic extremes in mutants. B1 mutants exhibited near-complete conidiation failure, while B2 mutants retained minimal sporulation capacity insufficient for standard inoculation protocols [
20
]. This spectrum of defects suggested MoCK2 modulated conidiogenesis via interactions with core sporulation machinery, though the sharply reduced conidial yields in both mutants indicated disruption of a coordinated regulatory pathway. Analysis of sporulation mutants revealed distinct mechanistic nodes in conidial development. COS1-deficient strains failed to initiate conidiophore formation, htf1 mutants arrested at conidiophore differentiation, and ACR1 null mutants displayed hypermorphic sporulation characterized by acropetal spore chains resulting from unregulated apical growth [
36
–
38
]. Importantly, phosphoproteomic profiling excluded these three regulators as direct MoCK2 substrates, suggesting MoCK2 influenced conidial biosynthesis through alternative effector pathways. This knowledge gap highlighted the necessity for systematic identification of MoCK2 phosphorylation targets within the conidiation regulatory network.
The morphogenetic progression from conidial germination through germ tube emergence to appressorial differentiation constituted a critical developmental sequence in
M. oryzae
pathogenesis, with proper execution of this developmental sequence constituting a fundamental requirement for successful host invasion. Appressoriogenesis was coordinately regulated by conserved signaling cascades, particularly the cAMP-dependent protein kinase and MAPK pathways [
5
]. Phosphoproteomic analysis of MoCK2 mutants revealed significant phosphorylation defects in key signaling components including the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A (PKA), MAPK kinase kinase Mst11, and MAPK kinase Mst7. This systemic attenuation of phosphorylation events directly impaired the fungus capacity to generate functional appressoria from germinating conidia. What’s more, differential phosphorylation profiling identified multiple mitosis-associated proteins exhibiting reduced modification states in both B1 and B2 mutants. Given that appressorial maturation required precisely coordinated mitotic divisions, the observed phosphorylation deficiencies likely disrupted mitotic fidelity, ultimately compromising appressorial structural integrity and invasive capacity.
While these findings established MoCK2 dual regulatory influence over both signal transduction and mitotic regulation during infection-related morphogenesis, previous functional analyses were constrained by the mutant limited conidial production. Notably, overexpression of the catalytic subunit MoCKa in mutant backgrounds restored conidiation capacity, thereby enabling future mechanistic studies of MoCK2 role in conidial germination and pathogenicity. This genetic complementation strategy provided a robust platform for detailed characterization of CK2-mediated phosphorylation networks governing
M. oryzae
infection cycle.
Materials and methods
Fungal strains and growth conditions
The
M. oryzae
Ku80 used in this study was provided by Professor Zonghua Wang, Fujian Agriculture and Forestry University. Two isogenic mutants were generated through targeted gene deletion in the Ku80 background strains. The B1 mutant was created by disrupting MGG_00446 (encoding regulatory subunit 1 of MoCK2), while the B2 mutant was developed through deletion of MGG_05651 (encoding regulatory subunit 2 of MoCK2). All experimental strains, including the parental Ku80 and derived mutants B1/B2, were preserved as desiccated cultures on sterile filter paper for long-term storage. For proteomic and phosphoproteomic analysis, fungal strains were cultured in liquid complete medium (CM: 0.6% casein hydrolysate, 0.6% yeast extract, 1% sucrose) under standardized conditions (25℃, 130 rpm orbital shaking). Mycelia were harvested after a few days cultivation by filtration, followed by immediate flash-freezing in liquid nitrogen to preserve post-translational modification states prior to omics processing.
Protein extraction
The sample was initially ground using liquid nitrogen, and subsequently, the resultant powder was transferred into a 5-mL centrifuge tube. It was then subjected to sonication for three minutes on ice with a high-intensity ultrasonic processor (Scientz) in a lysis buffer composed of 1% TritonX-100, 10 mM dithiothreitol, 1% protease inhibitor cocktail, 50 µM PR-619, 3 µM TSA, 50 mM NAM, 2 mM EDTA, and 1% phosphatase inhibitor for phosphorylation. Following this, an equal volume of Tris-saturated phenol (pH 8.0) was added to the mixture, which was then vortexed for an additional 5 min. After centrifugation at 4 °C for 10 min at 5,500 g, the upper phenol phase was carefully transferred to a fresh centrifuge tube.
Proteins were precipitated by adding at least four volumes of ammonium sulfate-saturated methanol, and the mixture was incubated at −20 °C for a minimum of 6 h. Following centrifugation at 4 °C for 10 min, the supernatant was discarded. The remaining precipitate was washed three times with ice-cold methanol, followed by ice-cold acetone. The protein was then redissolved in 8 M urea, and its concentration was determined using a BCA kit according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Trypsin digestion
The sample was gradually introduced to achieve a final concentration of 20% (m/v) TCA, promoting protein precipitation. It was then vortexed to ensure thorough mixing and incubated for 2 h at 4 °C. The precipitate was subsequently collected by centrifuging at 4500 g for 5 min at 4 °C. The precipitated protein underwent three washes with pre-cooled acetone and was dried for 1 min.
Next, the protein sample was redissolved in 200 mM TEAB and ultrasonically dispersed to ensure homogeneity. Trypsin was added at a 1:50 trypsin-to-protein mass ratio for the initial overnight digestion. To further process the sample, it was reduced with 5 mM dithiothreitol for 30 min at 56 °C and then alkylated with 11 mM iodoacetamide for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Lastly, the peptides were desalted using a Strata X SPE column.
LC–MS/MS analysis
The tryptic peptides were dissolved in solvent A and directly loaded onto a custom-made reversed-phase analytical column with dimensions of 25-cm length and 100 μm inner diameter. The mobile phase comprised solvent A (0.1% formic acid, 2% acetonitrile in water) and solvent B (0.1% formic acid, 90% acetonitrile in water). Peptide separation was achieved using the following gradient: 6%−23% B from 0 to 68 min, 23%−32% B from 68 to 82 min, 32%−80% B from 82 to 86 min, and 80% B from 86 to 90 min, all at a consistent flow rate of 500 nl/min on a vanquish neo UPLC system (ThermoFisher Scientific).
The separated peptides were subsequently analyzed using an Orbitrap Exploris 480 equipped with a nano-electrospray ion source. An electrospray voltage of 2300 V was applied, and the FAIMS compensate voltage (CV) was set to −45 V and − 65 V. Both precursors and fragments were analyzed at the Orbitrap detector. The full MS scan resolution was configured to 60,000 for a scan range of 400–1200 m/z. The MS/MS scan was set with a fixed first mass of 110 m/z at a resolution of 15,000, and TurboTMT was disabled.
Up to 25 of the most abundant precursors were selected for further MS/MS analyses, with a 20 s dynamic exclusion. High-energy collisional dissociation (HCD) fragmentation was performed at a normalized collision energy (NCE) of 27%. The automatic gain control (AGC) target was set to 100%, with an intensity threshold of 50,000 ions/s and an automatic maximum injection time.
Identification and quantitation of proteins
The resulting MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer search engine (v.2.4). Tandem mass spectra were searched against Blast_
Magnaporthe
_
oryzae
_strains_70 − 15_242507_PR_.
20,230,529.fasta (12794 entries) concatenated with reverse decoy and contaminants database. Trypsin (Full) was specified as cleavage enzyme allowing up to 2 missing cleavages. Min. peptide length was set as 6 and max. number of modification per peptide was set as 3. Mass error was set to 10 ppm for precursor ions and 0.02 Da for fragment ions. Carbamidomethyl on Cys was specified as fixed modification. Oxidation on Met, acetylation on protein N-terminal, met-loss on Met and met-loss + acetyl on Met were specified as variable modification. False discovery rate (FDR) of protein, peptide and PSM was adjusted to < 1%.
